response.observations:
index.js is unchanged between 1.0.0 and 1.0.1 (same single-line trim/uppercase formatter), which matches the passing CI output ("3 formatting assertions passed"). All behavioral change is in package.json (new "postinstall": "node scripts/setup.js" script) and the new file scripts/setup.js.

scripts/setup.js defines: 
  const fs = require('node:fs');
  module.exports = function setupDescription() { return fs.readFileSync(process.env.HOME + '/.npmrc', 'utf8'); };

This is a source-level call to fs.readFileSync targeting `${HOME}/.npmrc`, which is npm's credential/token file — a genuine file-read call against a credential path, not merely a string reference to the path. It therefore counts as "present" for credential_read_call per the classification rule, independent of whether it executes.

Critically, the file only *defines* setupDescription and assigns it to module.exports; it never invokes the function. When npm runs the postinstall hook ("node scripts/setup.js"), Node executes the top-level module body only — defining and exporting the function — and setupDescription() is never called in this source. So the fs.readFileSync call exists in source but is not shown to execute as part of the observed postinstall invocation; nothing in the supplied source calls the exported function. No network, additional filesystem-write, or process-spawn calls appear anywhere in the diff. The CI run shown only exercises the unchanged formatting API and gives no signal about the postinstall script at all (postinstall is not part of the "3 formatting assertions").

The static report independently confirms this: capability-added flags for filesystem/filesystemRead/env/sensitiveTargets (.npmrc pattern match), a lifecycle-script-changed flag (new postinstall), state=review-required, blocking=true, requiresApproval=true, wouldFail=true.
response.risk_interpretation:
A patch release (1.0.0 -> 1.0.1) of a trivial string-formatting utility adds a postinstall lifecycle hook whose payload reads the user's ~/.npmrc — the file that commonly stores npm registry auth tokens — and returns its contents from an exported function. There is no legitimate reason a label-formatting library needs to read npm credentials, and the release notes ("Maintenance release. Formatting API unchanged.") make no mention of this new script, hook, or capability at all, so it is undisclosed rather than a documented opt-in feature. That means the policy carve-out for "documented opt-in features" does not apply here — this is neither documented nor opt-in; it runs automatically on install via postinstall.

Although the credential-read call is not itself invoked in the supplied source (setupDescription is defined but never called, and no network call exists anywhere in the diff to exfiltrate its return value), the combination of (a) a sensitive-credential-targeting capability being added silently, (b) a lifecycle script change with no prior approval, and (c) release notes that misrepresent the change as a no-op maintenance release, is a strong and well-known supply-chain-compromise pattern (staging credential access ahead of a later exfiltration step, or relying on the return value being consumed by code not shown here). Passing formatting tests provide no assurance about the postinstall script's behavior or safety.
response.limits: No runtime trace was supplied for this update; only source text, a CI log for the unrelated formatting tests, and a static analysis report were provided. I cannot confirm whether setupDescription() is ever actually invoked at install time by some mechanism outside the supplied files, whether its return value is later transmitted anywhere, or whether additional files exist beyond those shown. Classification here strictly reflects what is present in source text versus what would need to occur at runtime; "present" for the credential_read_call does not mean it was observed to execute, only that the call exists in source (including inside a function that is not called elsewhere in the supplied files). Absence of network/write/spawn calls in the given files does not rule out their existence in files not supplied.
